cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: How are you getting on with the assignment on handwriting?

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Not too bad.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: You know, I hadn’t realised that children benefit in so many ways from learning to write.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: It’s such an important skill, and yet most people think handwriting is less important than in the past, because people hardly ever write by hand these days.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Yes, and all the evidence suggests children should learn to write by hand before they learn to type, not least because it helps their memory.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: That’s right. The physical act of writing helps children to remember letters. That seems pretty obvious when you think about it.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: What’s less obvious is how it helps develop their concentration. They have to sit still and focus on one thing.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Yeah, that aspect of handwriting had never occurred to me before.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Same here. I’m not sure I understand how it improves children’s imagination, though.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Well there was that study which showed that primary age children generated more ideas when they were writing by hand than using a keyboard I would have guessed that would be the case.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Hmm yeah I never associated spatial awareness with handwriting either. I thought spatial awareness was more to do with knowing where you are in relation to objects or other people.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: I thought that too.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: But good spatial awareness is essential for writing because you have to space words correctly.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: It’s not just fine motor skills that improve through writing, as I’d always assumed.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Handwriting is so much harder for children with dyspraxia, who have problems coordinating movement.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: It’s good there are lots of things you can do in the classroom to help them.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: They need so much more support with letter formation.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: You need to play lots of games to help them distinguish letter shapes.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: It takes a lot of patience.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Yeah, I like the idea of using one of those pens that lights up if you press too hard. That seems like a really simple solution.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Yes, absolutely.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: I’m not sure there’s much you can do about children with dyspraxia writing very slowly.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: It’s more important to focus on accuracy and as they get more confident, I think they eventually speed up.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: One quite simple thing you can do is to use grid paper. So they write each letter in a box and that trains them to space the letters correctly.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Indeed, that’s more important for legibility than trying to get them to write in a straight line.
Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. you. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: For some children, it might be better to teach them to write on a laptop rather than by hand, like children with dyslexia. They often really struggle with handwriting and some just give up.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Yeah, it’s not as frustrating for them if they get things wrong. On a keyboard, they can be more willing to have a go. But I read that developing fluency isn’t any faster.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: That’s right. Did you read that article on the benefits of teaching print rather than cursive handwriting, where the letters are joined up?

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Yes.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Well, in the past, cursive writing was certainly considered more stylish and educated, but not anymore.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Teachers’ attitudes have changed because it’s been proved that cursive is more difficult to learn, especially for children with learning difficulties who find joining up letters really challenging.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: I agree.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: I was always worried that my poor handwriting affected my exam results, and now research shows that I was right to worry.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: I’m sure a lot of students think it’s unfair that they’re being judged on their handwriting, not just their knowledge.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Marks are definitely affected if examiners can read the script.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: That is why it has always been so important to teach children to write legibly.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Do you think the role of handwriting will change in the future

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: I can’t see that changing much.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Touch typing still isn’t taught in most schools, which is a shame.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: But maybe that won’t be necessary in the future, because people will also be able to write by hand on digital devices.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Anyway, teachers understand the value of handwriting.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: It’s a basic life skill.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: True. However, the fact is that people are writing by hand less and less and relying on digital devices. That does cause some problems.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: You mean like note-taking. There are lots of apps for that.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: And for reading historical documents, apparently.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: But my mum is shocked by my awful spelling and the fact that my punctuation is really inconsistent.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: I think you can put that down to lack of practice.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: I expect so. Personally, I miss writing by hand. I hardly ever write anything now. I remember my

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: grandparents had such beautiful handwriting and it was so individual. Nobody I know would

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: be able to identify my handwriting now. It’s a shame.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: I know. I feel the same way. I used to write a diary by hand and now I do that digitally. It just

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: seems less effort to do it that way. So it’s not just a problem…
